extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers; Royal Society members; practitioners replicating 17th-century optics and pneumatics experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Instructions and evaluative criteria for reproducing and reporting Newton's prism (optics) experiments (and related guidance on vacuum/pneumatical experiments). Focuses on experimental setup, observations to expect, how to distinguish artefacts, and what to record when reporting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism positioning and basic setup
rubrics_metrics.description: How to hold and place the prism: take any prism and hold it so that its axis is perpendicular to the sun's rays; place it as close as may be to the hole through which the sun shines into a dark room (hole ~ size of a pea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn the prism slowly about its axis; when the colours move to the middle (nearest the place the sun's direct ray would pass), stop so the rays are equally refracted on both sides. In open window trials the prism should be placed close to the hole so the sun's light that comes through the hole also passes through the prism. If testing in a dark room, use a small round hole in a paper immediately before the prism (suggested ~1/4 or 1/8 inch) so the sun may shine through it; place the wall or paper 15–20 feet (or further) from the prism to observe the figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected figure and colour ordering in the primary image
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary/relevant image is oblong (not round) with colours succeeding in order red, yellow, green, blue, purple (red at one end, violet at the other, bluish green in the middle). Its length is transverse to the axis of the prism (or described as 'the length ... being not parallel but transverse to the axis of the prism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oblongness increases with (a) larger prism angle (refracting planes), and (b) greater distance from prism to illuminated surface. The image may be made more conspicuous by darkening the room (draw curtains). Observe that the oblong image is produced by two refractions only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing the three images produced by a prism
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three different images a prism can cast which must not be confused: (1) an oblong, vividly coloured image made by two refractions only (the primary image); (2) an image made by two refractions plus an intervening reflection, which is round and colourless if the reflecting base angles are equal but may be coloured if unequal; (3) an image made by a single reflection, always round and colourless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The danger is mistaking the second (or third) image for the first. They are distinguishable not only by shape and colour but also by their motion when the prism is rotated: the second and third images move swiftly and always in the same direction until they disappear; the first moves slowly, becomes stationary, then reverses direction and returns to its origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental motion/behaviour diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviour of images under continuous rotation of the prism: the primary (two-refraction) image moves slowly, becomes stationary, then reverses; the other images (involving reflections) move swiftly and travel steadily until they vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the difference in motion as a practical diagnostic to identify the primary image in contested or ambiguous trials (important when multiple images are visible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural replication checklist and reporting requirements (prism)
rubrics_metrics.description: What to record and report when reproducing the prism experiment: detailed dimensions and positions so differences in experimental practice can be identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report length, breadth, and figure of the illuminated space; length, breadth, and angles of the prism; prism position relative to incident rays and to the window shutter; largeness of the hole in the shutter; which side of the prism the sun shone on and on which side the light emerged; distance from prism to opposite paper/wall where refracted light is cast perpendicularly; situation of each colour within the figure. If possible, illustrate with one or two schemes/diagrams. This level of description enables diagnosis of experimental failure and rectification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility / dispute resolution principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes about experimental claims (e.g., whether an experiment 'succeeds' as described) are to be decided by new trials and demonstration rather than rhetorical dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite challengers to try the experiment under the author's directions (and to show their method if they claim different results); demonstrate at society meetings; try the experiment both in open light (clear day) and in a darkened room using the prescribed hole sizes and prism positions. Offer to show the experiment 'upon the least hint' to settle disagreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacuum (receiver) experiment setup and measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for testing the effect of vacuum on preservation: enclose specimens (fruit, meat, flowers, bread, butter) in receivers evacuated of air, sometimes with a little water to promote corruption, and include a gauge to detect air production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small or large receivers and note differences; use different sealing methods (cement vs skin) and observe their influence (cement smell can transfer to contents). Place a gauge (e.g., 4 inches long or mercury gauge) to track any air or gas produced (mercury rise indicates gas). Observe over defined intervals (hours, days, weeks, months) and record physical changes (withering, colour change, smell, taste), fermentation (bubbles in surrounding turpentine or lifting of cover), bursting of fruits, and smell development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls and variables for vacuum preservation studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential comparisons and variables to include: same specimens enclosed with air vs in vacuum; receiver size; sealing method; presence of water; whether the room is darkened; and inclusion of gauges to measure gas production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from trial outcomes: roses in vacuum with water showed little change and retained scent longer than roses enclosed with air (which grew mouldy in <3 days); small receivers often preserved fruit better than large ones; some fruits fermented and produced gas sufficient to lift covers; roasted vs raw meats show different gas production and smells; butter in vacuum smelled stronger but remained edible compared to butter kept in air. These controls help interpret whether preservation differences are due to vacuum, fermentation, sealing materials, or container size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation criteria for vacuum experiment outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: How to interpret signs of preservation or spoilage when specimens are kept in vacuo: use of physical signs (withering, swelling, bursting), chemical indicators (smell, taste), and mechanical evidence (gauge rise, cover lifting, gas bubbles) to infer fermentation, gas production, or decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bubbles forming in turpentine at the seal and lifting of covers indicate fermentation/gas production; burst cherries indicate internal gas pressure; changes in smell (rank, stronger) denote spoilage even if outward appearance remains; presence of water inside receiver can promote corrosion/rot. Note that absence of immediate change does not preclude later spoilage (e.g., many fruits showed little change for days but rotted rapidly after a point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy for the experimental method over disputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical/epistemic standard: favour experimental demonstration, reduction to natural causes, and empirical verification rather than scholastic disputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sturmius (and the book-review passage) emphasize teaching and publishing experiments reduced 'to causes' by demonstrative method, collecting notable modern experiments, and using experiment-centered instruction to advance natural philosophy. This is a criterion for the quality and acceptability of contributions: they should be experimental, demonstrative, and grounded in observable causes.
